text: Mainly because it affects our emotions faster than almost anything else. A few notes can make you feel calm, energetic or nostalgic within seconds. Music also connects people — every culture has songs for weddings, celebrations and grief. So I'd say it isn't just entertainment; it's one of the oldest ways humans have of sharing feelings.

text: It depends on the person and the task. For repetitive work, like tidying or data entry, music makes time pass faster and improves mood. But for reading or writing, songs with lyrics usually distract people, because the brain tries to process the words. Many students I know listen to instrumental music or quiet background sounds instead, which seems to work well.

text: I think it should be, at least in primary school. Learning an instrument develops concentration, memory and patience, and singing together teaches children to cooperate. Unfortunately, music lessons are often the first thing schools cut when budgets are tight. In Kazakhstan, it would also be a good way to make sure every child learns a few traditional songs and the basics of the dombra.

text: Probably because the teenage years are full of strong emotions and first experiences, and music becomes attached to those memories. A song from that time can bring back a whole summer or a group of friends. Also, as people get older and busier, they have less time to discover new music, so they naturally go back to what they already know.

text: Quiet music can make a place feel more welcoming, and studies suggest it can even change how long people stay in a shop. But it's often too loud or badly chosen, which is annoying if you're trying to talk or think. I think public places like libraries, hospitals and public transport should stay quiet, because not everyone wants a soundtrack to their day.
